 Credit: Far Out / Gage Skidmore In 2001, Harrison Ford thought audiences were sick of him. He was right, his next movie lost over $100 million
 Scott Campbell November 6th, 2026 · 8:15pm GMT Follow us on Google Discover When you’ve been as big a star for as long as Harrison Ford , you’re allowed to take the occasional risk now and then, even if you know that your core audience won’t show up to watch it on the big screen.
 He’d have loved them to, obviously, as any actor would, but he nonetheless had the sneaking suspicion that deviating so far from the type that made him a household name could realistically only lead to one of two outcomes, and even at that, he may have been surprised by how things turned out.
 For the bulk of his leading man career, viewers wanted to see Harrison Ford do Harrison Ford things , which is why the eight highest-grossing movies he’s ever played a leading role in found him as either Han Solo or Indiana Jones, with The Fugitive and Air Force One rounding out the top ten.
 It’s harder for a big name to lure paying customers to their local multiplex if they’re not doing the very thing that put their name above the marquee in the first place, and as much as he believed in the project, executive-producing in what was his first-ever behind-the-scenes credit, K-19: The Widowmaker was a flop, and even when shooting it between February and June 2001, Ford had a feeling.
 “There are actors who are able to disappear in a character, and they are called character actors and their parts, character parts,” the living legend reasoned. “I have been lucky to stumble into the role of the leading man; lucky, in that every picture needs one.” Lucky, yes, but luck only stretches so far.
 “That job has its own rules,” Ford went on. “It has its own utility and object that is different to the character actor. I enjoy character parts when they come my way, like the captain in K-19: The Widowmaker . The audience is manifestly less interested in seeing me do that kind of work.”
 That might be an understatement, if anything. While the historical thriller made history as the first $100million production to be directed by a woman, Kathryn Bigelow’s period-set submarine story lived up to expectations in one way only, by sinking without a trace to the bottom of the box office ocean.

 It’s not a terrible movie, by any means, but it’s not a particularly good one, either. Not even the goodwill generated by decades spent as one of the most reliable draws in the industry could save it, but, based on his feelings about what he knew audiences expected and wanted to see from him, he couldn’t have been surprised.
 Then again, maybe he was surprised, because K-19 lost an awful lot of money. Generous estimates put the picture at around $100million in the red when all was said and done, making it one of the most cataclysmic failures of the early 2000s, although Ford might have seen it coming from a mile off.
